title: This designer in Côte d’Ivoire is tailor-made to suit dignitaries
text:
This designer in Côte d’Ivoire is tailor-made to suit dignitaries
Promoting African designers is part of the wider mission of Pathé’O – starting with himself.
As the rhythmic clicking of a dozen sewing machines echoes through his small workshop, Ainé Pathé Ouédraogo weaves through the room, checking seams and hems. He holds a piece of multicolored tie-dye fabric up to the light, checking each stitch.
When you’re dressing the likes of Nelson Mandela, everything must be perfect.
The designer, known widely as Pathé’O, never thought he’d end up here – owning his own clothing brand or making custom clothing for celebrities and African heads of state. Growing up in a village in colonial Burkina Faso in the 1950s, he didn’t dare to dream big. “You’re just trying to survive one day to the next,” he recalls.
The fashion designer known as Pathé’O never thought he’d end up owning his own clothing brand or making custom clothing for celebrities and African heads of state. Growing up in a village in colonial Burkina Faso in the 1950s, he didn’t dare to dream that big. Now, he has own shop in the working-class Abidjan neighborhood of Treichville.
He credits his success to hard work. As a child, he picked wheat on Burkinabé plantations to scrape money together for his family, before following an older brother to Côte d’Ivoire. Once in the capital, Abidjan, Pathé’O took an apprenticeship with a Senegalese designer, learning how to tailor clothing while teaching himself new techniques.
Although he still hadn’t earned any money from his own work, Pathé’O was beginning to realize he had a special talent. “I remember making a piece of clothing, and the client looked down at me, this kid, and said, ‘You made this?’” says Pathé’O. “He couldn’t believe it.”
He eventually opened his own shop in the working-class Abidjan neighborhood of Treichville, but says he had to “fight to prove himself” as a tailor every day.
In 1987, Pathé’O won Cote d’Ivoire’s first Ciseaux d’Or – Golden Scissors – competition. But he didn’t get his big break until 1994, when Mandela was seen wearing one of his shirts – a gift from South African singer Miriam Makeba. He has since dressed African dignitaries, from Morocco’s King Mohammed VI to Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote, Africa’s wealthiest man. In 2019, Pathé’O offered Pope Francis a piece of his fabric during an interreligious peace delegation at the Vatican.
“It’s an honor and a privilege to wear his clothes,” says Djeny Diarra, a fashion blogger who recently visited Pathé’O’s shop, across the street from his atelier.
Selecting an outfit from Pathé’O’s many colors and styles is a formidable task. Each piece of cotton used in his designs is dyed individually, by hand, to produce the mottled pattern that has become his calling card. Instead of discarding leftover fabric, he turns the scraps into swaths of patchwork. Pathé’O estimates that his employees have produced 300 unique motifs.
Unlike many brand designers, Pathé’O has kept his prices reasonable, allowing him to share his creations with the wider public. Promoting African designers is, he says, part of his wider mission – starting with himself.
“I wear my clothes every day,” he says. “Of course.”
